passage:
For two weeks Noor let the sharp remarks in stand-ups slide. Ramesh would say, "Some of us actually read the ticket," and Sachin would go quiet. Noor told herself it would blow over. Instead the team began sitting on different sides of the table, and Sachin's screen kept showing job listings.

Finally Noor booked two private chats. She asked Ramesh what happened on release day and what he needed, then asked Sachin the same. Both talked for a long time, and both said nobody had asked before.

Next morning she stood at the whiteboard. Why did the release slip? Because both had shipped the fix. Why both? Because each believed the task was theirs. Why? Because two tickets carried the same name and nobody wrote a handover note. The quarrel was about the tickets, not about temperament.

In Sachin's chat a second thing had come out: Ramesh kept calling Sachin "the intern from the small college" in front of others. That was no mix-up over tasks. Noor wrote down dates and exact words, told both of them mediation would not be enough, and sent the notes to HR, as company process said.

qa.q: What did Ramesh say in the stand-ups?
qa.a: Ramesh said, "Some of us actually read the ticket."

qa.q: Why did waiting fail while the private chats and the whiteboard questions worked?
qa.a: Waiting let the tension spread until the team split and Sachin looked at job listings, whereas the chats made both feel heard and the repeated why-questions traced the blame to two tickets with the same name and no handover note.

qa.q: What was Sachin probably feeling while the remarks kept coming?
qa.a: Hurt and unheard: Sachin went quiet and kept looking at job listings.

qa.q: What could Noor do next to keep the ticket confusion from coming back?
qa.a: Noor could give each ticket one named owner and ask for a short handover note whenever work changes hands.

grounding: Four ways a lead handles one team conflict: ignoring it, listening separately, asking why repeatedly, and moving a conduct issue to HR.
